e.etymology: A modern American spelling of Davion, a name of the 1990s and 2000s in the family of Davon and Devion.
Persian parsa, pious or devout. The word's older history is uncertain; it is often linked to Pars, the old name of Persia.
A modern American coinage, a spelling of Braylee, which joins the Bray- of Brayden to the ending -lee.
A respelling of Kylie, a name that began in Australia, possibly from kylie, an Aboriginal word for a boomerang. Singer Kylie Minogue carried it around the English-speaking world.
In Finland a male name, first a pet form of Jalmari, the Finnish form of Hjalmar. American use for both boys and girls is probably independent, in the style of Jahari and Amari.
A modern name built on Tiana or clipped from Tatiana. It drew notice in the mid-2000s through Atiana De La Hoya, seen on the reality show Meet the Barkers.
A respelling of Riley, which comes both from an English place name meaning rye clearing and from the Irish surname O'Reilly, descendant of Raghallach.
A modern American name that extends Amari or Amara with the -iya ending of Aaliyah and Mariya. It also matches the sound of the biblical name Amariah.
Greek Barnabas, from Aramaic, probably son of the prophet; the Book of Acts explains it as son of encouragement. Barnabas was an early apostle who traveled with Paul.
namesakes: Barnabas Collins (vampire of the TV series Dark Shadows)

e.etymology: A Sicilian name from Greek kalogeros, literally beautiful in old age, the everyday Greek word for a monk. Saint Calogero was a hermit venerated across Sicily.
namesakes: Calogero Anello (the boy at the center of A Bronx Tale)

e.etymology: An Arabic name. Depending on how it is written in Arabic it is read as wakeful, one who stays up at night, or as enchanting.
Irish Riona, from Rionach, queenly, built on an old word for queen. It is also a short form of Catriona, and a separate Japanese girl's name is written Riona in English.
The French spelling of Abdul, from Arabic abd al-, servant of the, which opens names such as Abdullah, servant of God. It is common in French-speaking West Africa.
From Old Irish Fergus, built from fer, man, and gus, vigor or choice. Early Irish and Scottish kings bore it, as did Fergus mac Roich, a hero of the Ulster Cycle.
namesakes: King Fergus (Merida's father in Pixar's Brave)

e.etymology: A modern American name in the pattern of Aaliyah and Taliyah with an S opening.
The Italian and Spanish form of Valerius, a Roman family name from Latin valere, to be strong.
Given in Hebrew name books as a form of Erela, from erel, an angel. In the US it also reads as a shortened Ariella.
A West African form of Muhammad, from Arabic muhammad, praised or commendable. This French-influenced spelling is most common in Senegal and neighboring countries.
The Hebrew form of Manasseh. In Genesis, Joseph gives the name to his first son, saying God has made him forget his hardship. Manasseh became one of the tribes of Israel.
In Hasidic families Sura is the Yiddish form of Sarah, Hebrew for princess. Sura is also an Arabic girls' name, and sura is the word for a chapter of the Quran.
A modern American spelling in the family of Kalea, Kaleah and Khalia.
A spelling of Amelie, the French and German form of Amelia, from Germanic names beginning with amal, vigor or work. In the US it is used mostly in Spanish-speaking families, alongside Emely.
Arabic raghad, an easy and abundant life. The word appears in the Quran to describe eating freely in the garden.
The Turkish form of Karim, from Arabic karim, generous or noble. Al-Karim, the Generous, is one of the names of God in Islam.
A spelling of Yasir, from the Arabic root for ease and prosperity. Yasir ibn Amir was an early convert to Islam and the father of the companion Ammar.
From Arabic alam, world, carried through Persian into Bengali and Urdu, where it often forms part of longer names such as Shah Alam, king of the world.
A phonetic spelling of Nevaeh, the word heaven written backward, which became popular in the United States after 2000.
A spelling of Jiya, an Indian girls' name from Hindi jiya, heart or life. The -yah ending also fits American names such as Aaliyah and Amiyah.
A spelling of Zayden, an American name of the 2000s that sets a Z on the -ayden sound of Jayden, Kayden and Brayden.
The Yiddish form of Hebrew melech, king. It is often short for Elimelech, my God is king, a name honored among Hasidic families for Rabbi Elimelech of Lizhensk.
Arabic ilham, inspiration, especially the kind that comes from God. It is given to both girls and boys.
A spelling of Rosalie, the French form of Rosalia, from Latin rosa, rose. Saint Rosalia is the patron of Palermo.
